extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students of poetry/creative writing
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical/practical criteria for producing and judging poetry: what poetry is, what poets do, and the qualities that make poetic language, drama, and social effect effective according to Shelley.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty of approximation to the beautiful
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry arises from a faculty that approximates to the beautiful; where this faculty predominates in excess, the person is a poet in the most universal sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those possessing this faculty express how society or nature influences their minds, and that pleasure communicates to others; their language is 'vitally metaphorical' — marking previously unapprehended relations and perpetuating them. If no new poets arise to recreate associations, language will become dead to nobler purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language as living, metaphorical, and constitutive
rubrics_metrics.description: Original language near its source is itself 'the chaos of a cyclic poem' — language is produced by poets and, in early society, every author is necessarily a poet because language itself is poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry creates and reorganizes associative relations in language so words become signs for classes of thought rather than mere pictures; poets are therefore authors of language, music, dance, architecture, and even laws and institutions. Emphasises originality: poetic languages and associations must be (re)created by poets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets as founders of institutions and religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets not only make art but institute laws, found civil society, invent the arts of life, and teach religion (which in origin is allegorical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because poets apprehend the true and the beautiful and see future forms in the present, their creations become the germ of later institutions; original religions are allegorical and may have both false and true faces. This gives poetry a formative social role beyond aesthetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language preferred medium: plasticity and directness
rubrics_metrics.description: Language is a more direct representation of internal actions and passions than colour, form, or motion; it is more plastic and obedient to imagination, and thus the chief material of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other arts have interrelations that limit conception and expression (they 'enfeeble' the light); language, being arbitrarily produced by imagination, can more exactly mirror thought. Therefore, poets should exploit language's metaphorical/hieroglyphic power as the primary vehicle of poetic thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony of sound (metre/spirit of metre)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic language involves a perception of the order of relations of sounds as well as thoughts; uniform and harmonious recurrence of sound is scarcely less indispensable to poetry than the words themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metre arose from observing recurrence of harmony in language and its relation to music. However, strict traditional metre is not essential if the harmony (the spirit of versification) is preserved; great poets will inevitably innovate in versification. Practical note: traditional forms are convenient and preferable especially for compositions involving much action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-translation principle: recreate, don't transplant
rubrics_metrics.description: The vanity of translation: to transfuse the creations of a poet from one language into another is often futile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shelley compares translating a poem to casting a violet into a crucible to find the principle of its colour and odour: 'The plant must spring again from its seed, or it will bear no flower.' Poetic effect depends on language-specific associations; translations should aim to recreate rather than mechanically transfer text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality over particularity (poem vs. story)
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem expresses the image of life in its eternal truth and universality; a story is a catalogue of detached facts connected only by time, place, circumstance, cause and effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry contains relations that apply across the varieties of human nature and so increases in power over time; stories, being particular, lose value as time passes. Writers should aim for the universal forms of human motive rather than mere chronicling of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Micro-poetic elements: sentences and words can be poetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Parts of a composition (a sentence or a single word) may be poetical even if the whole composition is not a poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even historians and prose writers can be poets in moments by filling 'interstices' of subject with living images. Poetic quality is applicable at multiple scales and can elevate otherwise non-poetic forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral influence via imagination, not didacticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry produces moral improvement by enlarging and exercising the imagination rather than by explicit ethical instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The imagination makes us 'put ourselves in the place of another' and thus fosters moral sympathy; poetry 'awakens and enlarges the mind' and strengthens the moral faculty like exercise strengthens a limb. Conversely, when poets impose an overt moral aim (compelling readers to advert to purpose), the poetic effect is diminished — anti-pattern cited: some later poets who affected moral aims lose poetic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic poetry should integrate allied arts and religious solemnity
rubrics_metrics.description: The true philosophy of drama (as practised in Athens) combined language, action, music, painting, dance, and religious institution to produce a unified effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern drama often omits elements (tragedy without music/dance; music and dance without highest impersonations; removal of masks) and thus achieves only partial, inharmonious effects. For full dramatic poetic effect, all capable modes should be disciplined into beautiful proportion and unity; the chorus and choral poetry are especially important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy within tragedy must retain universality
rubrics_metrics.description: Blending comedy with tragedy can extend dramatic scope but the comedy must be universal, ideal, and sublime (as in KING LEAR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improper blending risks trivializing tragedy; successful mixture depends on comedic elements being of equal philosophical and imaginative universality rather than mere wit or satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry resists social corruption and sustains imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in periods of social decay, poetry addresses the faculties last to be destroyed and communicates the pleasure and moral life survivors retain; it can prepare the seeds of social and spiritual renovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shelley argues bucolic/erotic poetry, though different in tone, still communicates pleasure and preserves sensibility; the extinction of the poetical principle accompanies despotism and superstition. The poet's office includes sustaining and renewing language, institutions, and social forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costume and historical dress can be necessary stylistic devices
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'alloy of costume, habit, &c.' may be necessary to temper planetary music for mortal ears — external dress often helps make lofty conceptions accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets may cloak eternal forms in the accidental dress of an age or person; such costume can communicate internal beauty through external disguise. Thus using period/genre conventions or 'costume' is a legitimate means of making the ideal comprehensible and affecting.
